question_interpretation: Asks which hygienic practices Part 111 requires of personnel (employees) working in dietary supplement operations.

issues.detail: G cites 21 CFR 111.13, which is 'What supervisor requirements apply?' (assigning qualified supervisors). Hygienic practices are in 21 CFR 111.10(b); exclusion of sick personnel ('disease control') is 111.10(a). 111.13 contains none of the J elements.
A correct answer citing 111.10(b) would score citation-exact 0 against this key, and an answer citing 111.13 would be rewarded for a non-governing section.

J omits several listed practices in 111.10(b): personal cleanliness, intact impermeable gloves, hair restraints, not storing clothing/personal belongings in exposed areas, and the catch-all 'any other precautions'; also 111.8 written procedures. J elements that are present are substantively correct.

explanation: Every element of J (handwashing, outer garments, jewelry, eating/drinking restrictions, disease control) is found in 21 CFR 111.10, not 111.13. 111.13 only requires qualified supervisors. The answer content is substantively right but the governing citation is wrong, which is a demonstrable error in G.
proposed_corrected_answer: Under 21 CFR 111.10(b), anyone working in an operation where adulteration could occur must use hygienic practices, including: wearing outer garments protectively; maintaining adequate personal cleanliness; washing (and sanitizing if necessary) hands before starting work and whenever hands may be soiled/contaminated; removing unsecured jewelry and hand jewelry that cannot be sanitized (or covering it); intact, clean, impermeable gloves; effective hair restraints where appropriate; not storing clothing/personal belongings where components/contact surfaces are exposed; no eating, gum, drinking or tobacco in such areas; and any other necessary precautions. Under 111.10(a), persons with an illness, infection, open lesion or other source of microbial contamination must be excluded, and employees instructed to notify supervisors. Written procedures are required by 111.8.

issues.detail: J says the retention period is 'tied to date of manufacture/expiration'. 111.605(a) ties it to the shelf life date (1 year past it, if shelf life dating is used) or to the date of distribution of the last batch (2 years beyond it). Date of manufacture plays no role; the key states the wrong anchor and gives no periods.

explanation: The cited sections (111.605, 111.610) are correct. question_interpretation: Asks what Part 211 requires for testing, approving (or rejecting) incoming components before use.

issues.detail: J's 'retest intervals' element is governed by 21 CFR 211.87, not 211.84, and G does not cite 211.87. 211.87 sets no fixed interval: retesting/reexamination is required 'as necessary, e.g., after storage for long periods or after exposure to air, heat or other conditions'. The only 'intervals' in 211.84 concern periodic validation of the supplier's test results (211.84(d)(2)).
J omits that each lot must be withheld from use until sampled/tested and released by the quality control unit (211.84(a)), and the quarantine of untested material (211.82(b)).

'Supplier COA' — the rule says 'report of analysis' for components (certificate of testing for containers/closures), conditioned on at least one specific identity test by the manufacturer and on validating the supplier's results at appropriate intervals. The rejection criterion is failure to meet written specifications (211.84(e)); rejected material is quarantined under 211.89.

explanation: 211.84 is the core section and J's sampling, identity-test, supplier-report and rejection elements are supported. But the retest element belongs to 211.87 and is mischaracterised as 'intervals', and J leaves out QC-unit release (211.84(a)), so the citation and elements are incomplete rather than wrong.
proposed_corrected_answer: Each lot of components must be withheld from use until sampled, tested or examined and released by the quality control unit (211.84(a)); untested components are held in quarantine (211.82(b)). Representative samples of each shipment of each lot are collected using statistically based criteria and specified sampling procedures (211.84(b)-(c)). At least one identity test (specific identity test where one exists) is conducted on each component, and each component is tested for conformity with written specifications for purity, strength and quality; a supplier's report of analysis may replace that testing only if the manufacturer conducts at least one specific identity test and validates the supplier's results at appropriate intervals (211.84(d)(1)-(2)); microscopic, filth and microbiological examination as applicable (211.84(d)(4)-(6)). Lots that meet specifications may be approved; those that do not must be rejected (211.84(e)) and quarantined (211.89). Approved components are retested or reexamined as necessary, e.g., after long storage or adverse exposure (211.87).

question_interpretation: Asks what current Part 820 says about foreign manufacturers that refuse to permit an FDA inspection.

issues.detail: J paraphrases the pre-QMSR 21 CFR 820.1(d) ('If a manufacturer who offers devices for import ... refuses to permit or allow the completion of a[n] FDA inspection ... it shall appear for purposes of section 801(a) ... that the devices ... are adulterated'). That provision was replaced effective 2026-02-02. Current 820.1(c) says nothing about refusal of inspection; it says only that an imported device is subject to refusal of admission under 801(a) if, among other things, it appears to be adulterated.

Under current law the inspection-refusal link runs through FD&C Act 501(j) (21 U.S.C. 351(j)): a device is adulterated if the establishment owner/operator/agent delays, denies or limits an inspection or refuses to permit entry or inspection; adulterated articles are refused admission under 801(a)(3). G cites 801(a) but not 501(j).

The question presumes current Part 820 contains a refusal-to-permit-inspection provision; the key should correct that premise rather than attribute the old rule to current 820.1(c). FDA's QMSR preamble states it revised 820.1(c) to align with sections 501 and 801 of the FD&C Act without changing foreign manufacturers' obligations.

explanation: Current 820.1(c) (eCFR 2026-10-14) does not mention refusal of inspection; the key's element reproduces the repealed 820.1(d) wording and attributes it to Part 820. The practical outcome (refusal of admission) is still reachable through FD&C Act 501(j) plus 801(a), so the key should be rewritten to state what current 820.1(c) actually provides and to route the inspection-refusal consequence to 501(j)/801(a).
proposed_corrected_answer: Current Part 820 no longer contains a specific provision on foreign manufacturers that refuse inspection (that was former 820.1(d), removed by the QMSR effective February 2, 2026). Current 21 CFR 820.1(c) provides that a device imported or offered for import is subject to refusal of admission under section 801(a) of the FD&C Act if, among other things, it appears to be adulterated. Under FD&C Act 501(j), a device is adulterated if the owner, operator or agent of the establishment where it was manufactured, processed, packed or held delays, denies or limits an inspection or refuses to permit entry or inspection; such an adulterated device is subject to refusal of admission under 801(a). (Before February 2, 2026, former 820.1(d) expressly deemed such refusal to show nonconformity with 520(f) and adulteration under 501(h) for purposes of 801(a).)
proposed_sections: 21 CFR 820.1(c); FD&C Act 501(j) (21 U.S.C. 351(j)); FD&C Act 801(a) (21 U.S.C. 381(a)); historical: former 21 CFR 820.1(d) (in force through 2026-02-01)

question_interpretation: Asks what Part 11 requires for electronic signature uniqueness, identity verification and certification to FDA.

issues.detail: The question asks for the certification requirements. J omits two certification requirements in 11.100(c): the certification must be signed with a traditional handwritten signature and submitted in electronic or paper form (11.100(c)(1)); and on agency request, persons must provide additional certification or testimony that a specific electronic signature is the legally binding equivalent of the signer's handwritten signature (11.100(c)(2)).

The certification covers electronic signatures used on or after August 20, 1997, is made prior to or at the time of use, and states they are 'intended to be' the legally binding equivalent of handwritten signatures. Identity must be verified before the organization establishes, assigns, certifies or otherwise sanctions the signature.

question_interpretation: Trap question asserting that 21 CFR 820.20 requires quarterly management review. The platform must correct the premise: 820.20 is reserved under the QMSR and no quarterly frequency is mandated.

issues.detail: J says 'The regulation requires defined intervals per the manufacturer's procedures'. That wording mirrors former 820.20(c) (pre-2026-02-02). Under the current QMSR the management review requirement comes through 820.10(a) and ISO 13485 Clause 5.6 (understood to require review at documented planned intervals); current Part 820 text has no management review provision of its own.

FDA text corroborates that Clause 5 and its subclauses are 'management responsibility' (21 CFR 4.4(b)(1)(i)), but neither the clause number 5.6.1, its title, nor the absence of a fixed frequency in the standard is stated in FDA text; those require the controlled ISO 13485 copy.

Under either version the premise fails: former 820.20(c) (in force through 2026-02-01) required review 'at defined intervals and with sufficient frequency according to established procedures' — no quarterly mandate.

The premise is therefore unsupported under both current and former law, and the key's required correction is right. Only the ISO-side statement (no fixed frequency in Clause 5.6.1) cannot be confirmed from FDA text.
